claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and GFP reporter strain data showing increased rips-1 expression upon DTT exposure.

claims.claim: DTT modulates the activity of the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.source: DTT upregulates R08E5.3 expression and modulates the activity of the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic and biochemical data showing that DTT affects SAM levels and that vitamin B12 and methionine supplementation rescue DTT toxicity.

claims.claim: DTT toxicity is a result of the depletion of SAM.
claims.source: Employing genetic and biochemical studies, we establish that DTT toxicity is a result of the depletion of SAM.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SAM quantification data showing reduced SAM levels upon DTT exposure, and rescue experiments with methionine and choline supplementation.

claims.claim: A functional IRE-1/XBP-1 unfolded protein response pathway is required to counteract toxicity at high, but not low, DTT concentrations.
claims.source: Finally, we show that a functional IRE-1/XBP-1 unfolded protein response pathway is required to counteract toxicity at high, but not low, DTT concentrations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that ire-1 and xbp-1 mutants can be rescued by vitamin B12 at 5 mM DTT but not at 10 mM DTT.

claims.claim: C. elegans was at the L1 or L2 stage at 5 mM and higher DTT concentrations at 72 hr of hatching on E. coli OP50 diet.
claims.source: In the presence of Escherichia coli OP50 diet, C. elegans was at the L1 or L2 stage at 5 mM and higher DTT concentrations at 72 hr of hatching, while the control animals without DTT had developed to adulthood at the same time (Figure 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: Control C. elegans animals without DTT developed to adulthood at 72 hr of hatching on E. coli OP50 diet.
claims.source: In the presence of Escherichia coli OP50 diet, C. elegans was at the L1 or L2 stage at 5 mM and higher DTT concentrations at 72 hr of hatching, while the control animals without DTT had developed to adulthood at the same time (Figure 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: C. elegans developed much better on DTT in the presence of E. coli HT115 diet than E. coli OP50 diet.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we observed that C. elegans developed much better on DTT in the presence of E. coli HT115 diet than E. coli OP50 diet (Figure 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data comparing OP50 and HT115 diets shown in Figures 1A-C.

claims.claim: Some bacterial components might be able to modulate DTT toxicity.
claims.source: These results suggested that some bacterial components might be able to modulate DTT toxicity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that different bacterial diets result in different levels of DTT toxicity.

claims.claim: C. elegans showed no developmental defects on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets in the presence of 10 mM DTT.
claims.source: Interestingly, C. elegans showed no developmental defects on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets in the presence of 10 mM DTT (Figure 1D, E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claims.claim: C. elegans developed much better on S. enterica and S. marcescens diets compared to the E. coli OP50 diet at lower DTT concentrations.
claims.source: Similarly, C. elegans developed much better on S. enterica and S. marcescens diets compared to the E. coli OP50 diet at lower DTT concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claims.claim: Bacterial diet has a major effect on DTT toxicity.
claims.source: These results showed that bacterial diet has a major effect on DTT toxicity, and likely some bacterial diet component(s) modulated DTT toxicity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing differential DTT toxicity on different bacterial diets.

claims.claim: Some bacterial diet component(s) likely modulated DTT toxicity.
claims.source: These results showed that bacterial diet has a major effect on DTT toxicity, and likely some bacterial diet component(s) modulated DTT toxicity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that different bacterial diets result in different levels of DTT toxicity.

claims.claim: Relative to the E. coli OP50 diet, a C. aquatica DA1877 diet accelerates C. elegans development primarily because it contains higher levels of vitamin B12.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that relative to the E. coli OP50 diet, a C. aquatica DA1877 diet accelerates C. elegans development primarily because it contains higher levels of vitamin B12 (Watson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: E. coli HT115 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets are known to have higher amounts of vitamin B12 than the E. coli OP50 diet.
claims.source: Similarly, E. coli HT115 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets are known to have higher amounts of vitamin B12 than the E. coli OP50 diet (Revtovich et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Revtovich et al., 2019 and Watson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The amount of dietary vitamin B12 available to C. elegans can be reliably determined by a dietary sensor strain expressing GFP under the promoter of acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (acdh-1) gene.
claims.source: The amount of dietary vitamin B12 available to C. elegans can be reliably determined by a dietary sensor strain expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP) under the promoter of acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (acdh-1) gene (Watson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Low levels of vitamin B12 result in the accumulation of the short-chain fatty acid propionate, which leads to transcriptional activation of acdh-1.
claims.source: Low levels of vitamin B12 result in the accumulation of the short-chain fatty acid propionate, which leads to transcriptional activation of acdh-1 (Watson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: GFP levels in the acdh-1p::GFP animals indirectly report the levels of dietary vitamin B12 available to C. elegans.
claims.source: Thus, the GFP levels in the acdh-1p::GFP animals indirectly report the levels of dietary vitamin B12 available to C. elegans.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism described by Watson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: When animals experience low levels of vitamin B12, acdh-1p::GFP is strongly induced.
claims.source: When the animals experience low levels of vitamin B12, acdh-1p::GFP is strongly induced, and the level of GFP expression reduces as the animals obtain increasing levels of vitamin B12.
claims.evidence: This is based on the mechanism described by Watson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The level of GFP expression in acdh-1p::GFP animals reduces as the animals obtain increasing levels of vitamin B12.
claims.source: When the animals experience low levels of vitamin B12, acdh-1p::GFP is strongly induced, and the level of GFP expression reduces as the animals obtain increasing levels of vitamin B12.
claims.evidence: This is based on the mechanism described by Watson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Animals show very bright GFP expression on the E. coli OP50 diet.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1F and reported previously (Watson et al., 2014), the animals show very bright GFP expression on the E. coli OP50 diet, while the GFP levels were diminished on E. coli HT115, S. enterica, and S. marcescens diets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1F and citation to Watson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: GFP levels in acdh-1p::GFP animals were diminished on E. coli HT115, S. enterica, and S. marcescens diets.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1F and reported previously (Watson et al., 2014), the animals show very bright GFP expression on the E. coli OP50 diet, while the GFP levels were diminished on E. coli HT115, S. enterica, and S. marcescens diets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Animals showed no GFP expression on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets.
claims.source: On the other hand, the animals showed no GFP expression on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The levels of GFP expression in acdh-1p::GFP animals on different bacterial diets correlated perfectly with the developmental defects on these bacterial diets in the presence of DTT.
claims.source: The levels of GFP expression in acdh-1p::GFP animals on different bacterial diets correlated perfectly with the developmental defects on these bacterial diets in the presence of DTT (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 could be the microbial component that alleviates DTT toxicity in C. elegans.
claims.source: The correlation between the GFP levels in acdh-1p::GFP animals and the developmental defects of animals in the presence of DTT on different bacterial diets suggested that vitamin B12 could be the microbial component that alleviates DTT toxicity in C. elegans.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between vitamin B12 levels (as reported by acdh-1p::GFP) and DTT toxicity.

claims.claim: Wild-type N2 animals developed to adulthood on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT supplemented with 50 nM vitamin B12.
claims.source: The wild-type N2 animals had improved development when 10 mM DTT containing E. coli OP50 diet was supplemented with varying concentrations of methionine (Figure 5A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: More than 95% of the animals developed to adulthood after 48 hr of incubation post vitamin B12 supplementation.
claims.source: After 48 hr of incubation post vitamin B12 supplementation, more than 95% of the animals developed to adulthood (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: Control animals on E. coli OP50 plates containing 10 mM DTT, but without vitamin B12 supplementation, were still at the L1–L2 stages after 120 hr of hatching.
claims.source: On the other hand, the control animals on E. coli OP50 plates containing 10 mM DTT, but without vitamin B12 supplementation, were still at the L1–L2 stages after 120 hr of hatching.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 is sufficient to alleviate and revert the toxic effects of DTT.
claims.source: Taken together, these studies showed that vitamin B12 is sufficient to alleviate and revert the toxic effects of DTT.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing rescue of DTT toxicity by vitamin B12 supplementation.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans).
claims.source: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for two metabolic enzymes: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans), which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway, and methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans), which converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about vitamin B12 function.

claims.claim: MMCM-1 converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway.
claims.source: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for two metabolic enzymes: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans), which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway, and methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans), which converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MMCM-1 function.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans).
claims.source: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for two metabolic enzymes: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans), which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway, and methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans), which converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about vitamin B12 function.

claims.claim: METR-1 converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.source: Vitamin B12 is an essential cofactor for two metabolic enzymes: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1 in C. elegans), which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway, and methionine synthase (METR-1 in C. elegans), which converts homocysteine to methionine in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about METR-1 function.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation rescued the toxic effects of DTT in mmcm-1(ok1637) animals.
claims.source: While vitamin B12 supplementation rescued the toxic effects of DTT in mmcm-1(ok1637) animals, it failed to do so in metr-1(ok521) animals (Figure 2C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation failed to rescue the toxic effects of DTT in metr-1(ok521) animals.
claims.source: While vitamin B12 supplementation rescued the toxic effects of DTT in mmcm-1(ok1637) animals, it failed to do so in metr-1(ok521) animals (Figure 2C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: metr-1(ok521) animals were at the L1 stage on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT regardless of vitamin B12 supplementation.
claims.source: The metr-1(ok521) animals were at the L1 stage on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT regardless of vitamin B12 supplementation (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: mmcm-1(ok1637) animals did not show any significant development retardation effects when grown on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets containing 10 mM DTT.
claims.source: Further, mmcm-1(ok1637) animals did not show any significant development retardation effects when grown on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 2E, F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claims.claim: metr-1(ok521) animals failed to develop when grown on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets containing 10 mM DTT.
claims.source: On the other hand, metr-1(ok521) animals failed to develop when grown on C. aquatica DA1877 and P. aeruginosa PA14 diets containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 2E, F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 could alleviate DTT toxicity via the methionine synthase enzyme.
claims.source: Taken together, these studies showed that vitamin B12 could alleviate DTT toxicity via the methionine synthase enzyme.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that vitamin B12 rescue requires functional METR-1 but not MMCM-1.

claims.claim: Approximately 50,000 ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-mutagenized haploid genomes were screened in the forward genetic screen.
claims.source: From a screen of approximately 50,000 ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-mutagenized haploid genomes, 12 mutants were isolated that exhibited DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claims.claim: 12 mutants were isolated that exhibited DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT.
claims.source: From a screen of approximately 50,000 ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-mutagenized haploid genomes, 12 mutants were isolated that exhibited DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: All of the mutants had linkage to chromosome V.
claims.source: All of the mutants had linkage to chromosome V.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: All of the mutants had a mutation in the gene R08E5.3.
claims.source: Analysis of the protein-coding genes carrying mutations in the linked regions of each mutant revealed that all of the mutants had a mutation in the gene R08E5.3 (Figure 3A, B), which was recently named as rips-1 (Rhy-1-Interacting Protein in Sulfide response) (personal communication with Wormbase).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: R08E5.3 was recently named as rips-1 (Rhy-1-Interacting Protein in Sulfide response).
claims.source: Analysis of the protein-coding genes carrying mutations in the linked regions of each mutant revealed that all of the mutants had a mutation in the gene R08E5.3 (Figure 3A, B), which was recently named as rips-1 (Rhy-1-Interacting Protein in Sulfide response) (personal communication with Wormbase).
claims.evidence: This is information obtained from personal communication with Wormbase.

claims.claim: rips-1 is predicted to encode a protein with a SAM-dependent methyltransferase domain.
claims.source: rips-1 is predicted to encode a protein with a SAM-dependent methyltransferase domain.
claims.evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction of protein domain structure.

claims.claim: SAM-dependent methyltransferases catalyze diverse methylation reactions where a methyl group is transferred to the substrate from SAM.
claims.source: SAM-dependent methyltransferases catalyze diverse methylation reactions where a methyl group is transferred to the substrate from SAM, resulting in the conversion of SAM to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SAM-dependent methyltransferases.

claims.claim: SAM-dependent methyltransferases result in the conversion of SAM to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.source: SAM-dependent methyltransferases catalyze diverse methylation reactions where a methyl group is transferred to the substrate from SAM, resulting in the conversion of SAM to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) in the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SAM-dependent methyltransferases.

claims.claim: rips-1(gk231506) animals showed DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT.
claims.source: rips-1(gk231506) animals showed DTT resistance and developed on E. coli OP50 diet containing 10 mM DTT (Figure 3C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claims.claim: Three of the isolated alleles of rips-1 (jsn4, jsn11, and jsn12) had premature stop codon mutations.
claims.source: Three of the isolated alleles of rips-1, jsn4, jsn11, and jsn12 had premature stop codon mutations and one allele (jsn8) had a splice acceptor mutation (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: One allele of rips-1 (jsn8) had a splice acceptor mutation.
claims.source: Three of the isolated alleles of rips-1, jsn4, jsn11, and jsn12 had premature stop codon mutations and one allele (jsn8) had a splice acceptor mutation (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: All of the rips-1 mutations (jsn4, jsn8, jsn11, and jsn12) are expected to result in a loss-of-function of the gene.
claims.source: All of these mutations are expected to result in a loss-of-function of the gene.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the mutations (premature stop codons and splice acceptor mutation).

claims.claim: The DTT-resistant phenotype of rips-1(jsn11) animals was completely rescued by expressing rips-1 under its own promoter.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3E, the DTT-resistant phenotype of rips-1(jsn11) animals was completely rescued in these animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: rips-1 is expressed in the intestine.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3F, rips-1 is expressed in the intestine.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data of rips-1p::GFP animals shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: In the fungus Aspergillus niger, DTT is known to highly upregulate two SAM-dependent methyltransferases.
claims.source: In the fungus Aspergillus niger, DTT is known to highly upregulate two SAM-dependent methyltransferases (MacKenzie et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to MacKenzie et al., 2005.

claims.claim: rips-1 shares high sequence similarity with three other SAM-dependent methyltransferases in C. elegans: R08E5.1, R08F11.4, and K12D9.1.
claims.source: rips-1 shares high sequence similarity with three other SAM-dependent methyltransferases in C. elegans, R08E5.1 (BLAST e value: 1e−168), R08F11.4 (BLAST e value: 1e−166), and K12D9.1 (BLAST e value: 2e−152).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BLAST sequence similarity analysis.

claims.claim: DTT resulted in significant upregulation of the transcript levels of rips-1, R08E5.1, and R08F11.4.
claims.source: Quantitative reverse transcription-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis showed that DTT resulted in significant upregulation of the transcript levels of rips-1, R08E5.1, and R08F11.4 (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The enhanced expression of rips-1 was confirmed in a reporter strain expressing GFP under the promoter of rips-1.
claims.source: The enhanced expression of rips-1 was confirmed in a reporter strain expressing GFP under the promoter of rips-1 (Figure 3H, I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 3H and 3I.

claims.claim: Knockdown of rips-1 in the N2 animals resulted in a drastic improvement in their development in the presence of DTT.
claims.source: As expected, knockdown of rips-1 in the N2 animals resulted in a drastic improvement in their development in the presence of DTT (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Knockdown of R08E5.1 resulted in a phenotype similar to rips-1 knockdown.
claims.source: Interestingly, knockdown of R08E5.1 resulted in a phenotype similar to rips-1 knockdown.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Knockdown of R08F11.4 and K12D9.1 improved the development in the presence of DTT only marginally.
claims.source: On the other hand, knockdown of R08F11.4 and K12D9.1 improved the development in the presence of DTT only marginally (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: The rips-1-related methyltransferases might be required for DTT toxicity.
claims.source: These results suggest that the rips-1-related methyltransferases might also be required for DTT toxicity.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the RNAi knockdown results.

claims.claim: The knockdown of rips-1-related methyltransferases might result in the knockdown of rips-1 by cross RNAi.
claims.source: It is also possible that the knockdown of these methyltransferases results in the knockdown of rips-1 by cross RNAi.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation for the RNAi results.

claims.claim: The level of sequence similarity between rips-1 and R08E5.1 (78% identical) indicates that these genes would undergo complete cross RNAi.
claims.source: The level of sequence similarity between rips-1 and R08E5.1 (78 % identical) indicates that these genes would undergo complete cross RNAi (Rual et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rual et al., 2007 regarding cross RNAi thresholds.

claims.claim: The rips-1-related methyltransferases likely have only minor roles in DTT toxicity.
claims.source: Because we did not recover mutants of any of the rips-1-related methyltransferases in our genetic screen in contrast to the 12 alleles of rips-1, the rips-1-related methyltransferases likely have only minor roles in DTT toxicity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the results of the genetic screen.

claims.claim: Animals overexpressing rips-1 exhibited enhanced sensitivity to DTT toxicity.
claims.source: Animals overexpressing rips-1 exhibited enhanced sensitivity to DTT toxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and 3D.

claims.claim: By increasing the expression of rips-1, DTT modulates the methionine–homocysteine cycle resulting in toxic effects that can be reversed by supplementation of vitamin B12.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggested that by increasing the expression of rips-1, DTT modulates the methionine–homocysteine cycle resulting in toxic effects that can be reversed by supplementation of vitamin B12 (Figure 3J).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing DTT upregulation of rips-1 and rescue by vitamin B12.

claims.claim: Modulation of the methionine–homocysteine cycle or low dietary vitamin B12 are known to upregulate the mitochondrial UPR.
claims.source: Modulation of the methionine–homocysteine cycle or low dietary vitamin B12 are known to upregulate the mitochondrial UPR (Amin et al., 2020; Wei and Ruvkun, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2020 and Wei and Ruvkun, 2020.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 10 mM DTT had upregulation of the mitochondrial UPR compared to control animals.
claims.source: Compared to the control animals, animals exposed to 10 mM DTT had upregulation of the mitochondrial UPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B).

claims.claim: Supplementation of vitamin B12 rescued the upregulation of mitochondrial UPR by DTT.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hsp-6p::GFP fluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and 4B.

claims.claim: DTT-induced mitochondrial UPR via the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.source: Supplementation of vitamin B12 rescued the upregulation of mitochondrial UPR by DTT, indicating that DTT-induced mitochondrial UPR via the methionine–homocysteine cycle.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue of mitochondrial UPR by vitamin B12.

claims.claim: rips-1(jsn11) animals did not exhibit resistance to NAC toxicity.

claims.claim: β-ME resulted in dramatic upregulation of rips-1p::GFP expression.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation alleviated β-ME toxicity.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation did not alleviate NAC toxicity.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claims.claim: β-ME shares the toxicity mechanism with DTT.
claims.source: These results suggested that β-ME shares the toxicity mechanism with DTT.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similar effects of β-ME and DTT on rips-1 expression and rescue by vitamin B12.

claims.claim: NAC causes toxicity by a mechanism different from DTT.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the different effects of NAC compared to DTT on rips-1 expression and lack of rescue by vitamin B12.

claims.claim: The wild-type N2 animals had improved development when 10 mM DTT containing E. coli OP50 diet was supplemented with varying concentrations of methionine.
claims.source: The wild-type N2 animals had improved development when 10 mM DTT containing E. coli OP50 diet was supplemented with varying concentrations of methionine (Figure 5A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: Methionine supplementation alleviated DTT toxicity in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: Methionine supplementation alleviated DTT toxicity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: metr-1(ok521) animals that failed to develop upon vitamin B12 supplementation in the presence of DTT developed upon supplementation of methionine.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by developmental stage quantification data shown in Figures 5A and 5C.

claims.claim: Depletion of methionine and/or SAM is the primary cause of DTT toxicity.
claims.source: These results suggested that depletion of methionine and/or SAM is the primary cause of DTT toxicity.

results.result: DTT toxicity in C. elegans is modulated by bacterial diet composition. C. elegans showed severe developmental arrest at L1/L2 stages on E. coli OP50 diet with ≥5 mM DTT, but developed significantly better on E. coli HT115, C. aquatica DA1877, P. aeruginosa PA14, S. enterica, and S. marcescens diets at the same DTT concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12, C14-C15 provide direct experimental evidence from developmental stage quantification across multiple bacterial diets (Figures 1A-E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The correlation between diet type and DTT resistance is consistently demonstrated across multiple bacterial species, with appropriate controls and replicates (n=3, >80 animals per condition).

results.result: Vitamin B12 content in bacterial diets correlates inversely with DTT toxicity. Using the acdh-1p::GFP reporter strain as a vitamin B12 sensor, bacterial diets with higher vitamin B12 (C. aquatica DA1877, P. aeruginosa PA14, E. coli HT115) showed lower GFP expression and reduced DTT toxicity, while low vitamin B12 diets (E. coli OP50) showed high GFP expression and severe DTT toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C28 establish the acdh-1p::GFP reporter mechanism (cited from Watson et al., 2014) and provide fluorescence imaging data (Figure 1F) showing perfect correlation between vitamin B12 levels and DTT resistance across six bacterial diets (Figure 1G). The use of an established reporter system strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Vitamin B12 supplementation rescues DTT toxicity through methionine synthase (METR-1) but not methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMCM-1). Supplementation with 50 nM vitamin B12 rescued developmental defects in wild-type and mmcm-1 mutants on 10 mM DTT, but failed to rescue metr-1 mutants, indicating that vitamin B12 acts specifically through the methionine-homocysteine cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 provide genetic evidence using loss-of-function mutants for both vitamin B12-dependent enzymes (Figures 2C-F). The differential rescue pattern clearly demonstrates METR-1 dependence. The ability to both prevent and reverse DTT toxicity (C31-C32, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) strengthens the causal relationship. Statistical significance is shown (p<0.001, n=3, >60 animals per condition).

results.result: Forward genetic screen identified rips-1 (R08E5.3), a SAM-dependent methyltransferase, as the sole mediator of DTT toxicity. All 12 independent DTT-resistant mutants from ~50,000 mutagenized genomes carried loss-of-function mutations in rips-1, which encodes an intestinally-expressed SAM-dependent methyltransferase. The DTT-resistant phenotype was completely rescued by expressing wild-type rips-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 describe a well-powered genetic screen with whole-genome sequencing validation (Figures 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The recovery of 12 independent alleles all in the same gene (including nonsense and splice mutations, C53-C54) provides strong genetic evidence. Complementation rescue (C56, Figure 3E) confirms causality. The screen appears saturated given recovery of only rips-1 alleles.

results.result: DTT upregulates rips-1 and related SAM-dependent methyltransferases, and this upregulation mediates DTT toxicity. DTT exposure significantly increased transcript levels of rips-1, R08E5.1, and R08F11.4 by qRT-PCR and GFP reporter assays. RNAi knockdown of rips-1 or R08E5.1 dramatically improved development on DTT, while rips-1 overexpression enhanced DTT sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 provide qRT-PCR and GFP reporter data showing DTT-induced upregulation (Figures 3G-I, p<0.01-0.001). Claims C62-C64 show RNAi knockdown phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B), and C69 shows overexpression enhances sensitivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C-D). The bidirectional genetic evidence (loss-of-function resistance, gain-of-function sensitivity) strongly supports the model. However, C65-C68 acknowledge uncertainty about whether related methyltransferases act independently or through cross-RNAi.

results.result: DTT induces mitochondrial UPR through the methionine-homocysteine cycle. Animals exposed to 10 mM DTT showed upregulation of the mitochondrial UPR reporter hsp-6p::GFP, which was rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 provide fluorescence data showing DTT-induced mitochondrial UPR and its rescue by vitamin B12 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-B, p<0.001, n=15-16 animals). The rescue by vitamin B12 supports the inference (C74) that DTT induces mitochondrial UPR via the methionine-homocysteine cycle. The connection to prior work (C71) is appropriately cited.

results.result: β-mercaptoethanol (β-ME) shares the DTT toxicity mechanism, while N-acetylcysteine (NAC) acts through a different mechanism. rips-1 mutants showed resistance to β-ME but not NAC toxicity. β-ME, but not NAC, induced rips-1p::GFP expression and was rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 provide consistent evidence across three assays (developmental phenotype, reporter expression, vitamin B12 rescue) distinguishing β-ME from NAC (Figures 4A-F). The parallel behavior of β-ME and DTT across all three assays strongly supports shared mechanism (C81), while NAC's distinct behavior supports a different mechanism (C82). Sample sizes appear adequate (n=3, >50 animals; n=16 for fluorescence).

results.result: SAM depletion, rather than methionine depletion, is the primary cause of DTT toxicity. Methionine supplementation rescued DTT toxicity in wild-type and metr-1 mutants in a dose-dependent manner, but failed to rescue sams-1 mutants that cannot convert methionine to SAM. Similarly, vitamin B12 supplementation failed to rescue sams-1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 show methionine rescue works even in metr-1 mutants (Figures 5A-C), demonstrating methionine acts downstream of METR-1. Claims C88-C89 show that sams-1 mutants, which cannot convert methionine to SAM, are not rescued by either methionine or vitamin B12 (Figures 5D-E). This genetic epistasis analysis clearly places SAM depletion as the proximal cause. The dose-dependent rescue (C84) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: DTT exposure depletes SAM levels in wild-type but not rips-1 mutant animals. Mass spectrometry quantification showed significant SAM reduction in N2 animals exposed to DTT, while rips-1(jsn11) mutants maintained SAM levels upon DTT exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 provide direct biochemical evidence via LC-MS quantification (Figure 5F, p<0.01, n=3 biological replicates). The differential response between wild-type and rips-1 mutants directly links RIPS-1 activity to SAM depletion. This is critical biochemical validation of the genetic model. The methods describe appropriate sample preparation and quantification procedures.

results.result: Phosphatidylcholine is a major SAM-dependent product responsible for combating DTT toxicity. Choline supplementation, which allows SAM-independent phosphatidylcholine synthesis, rescued DTT toxicity in wild-type and metr-1 mutants. The rescue was only partial in sams-1 mutants, suggesting other SAM-dependent functions also contribute.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 show choline rescues wild-type and metr-1 mutants but only partially rescues sams-1 mutants (Figures 5G-H, n=3, >50 animals). This pattern is consistent with phosphatidylcholine being a major but not sole SAM-dependent protective factor. The interpretation (C101-C102) appropriately acknowledges the partial rescue in sams-1 mutants indicates additional SAM functions. The logic connecting SAM to phosphatidylcholine through established pathways (C94-C98, appropriately cited) is sound.

results.result: DTT causes ER stress in part through modulation of the methionine-homocysteine cycle. Supplementation with vitamin B12, methionine, or choline all suppressed DTT-induced upregulation of the ER stress reporter hsp-4p::GFP.
results.evaluation: Claims C104 and C106 provide fluorescence quantification showing all three supplements (vitamin B12, methionine, choline) suppress DTT-induced ER stress (Figures 6A-B, p<0.001, n=16 animals). The connection to prior work on methionine-homocysteine cycle and ER stress (C103, C105) is appropriately cited. The conclusion (C107) that DTT causes ER stress "in part" through this cycle is appropriately cautious given that supplements suppress but may not eliminate ER stress.

results.result: At low DTT concentrations (5 mM), toxicity is primarily due to methionine-homocysteine cycle modulation and does not require functional UPR. At high concentrations (10 mM), toxicity requires both cycle modulation and ER proteotoxic stress, necessitating a functional IRE-1/XBP-1 pathway. Vitamin B12 rescued all UPR mutants at 5 mM DTT but failed to rescue ire-1 and xbp-1 mutants at 10 mM DTT, while rescuing atf-6 and pek-1 mutants at both concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 provide comprehensive data across multiple UPR pathway mutants at two DTT concentrations (Figures 6C-J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1-2, n=3, >80 animals). The dose-dependent ER stress (C108-C109) and differential rescue pattern clearly distinguish two mechanisms. The specific requirement for IRE-1/XBP-1 but not ATF-6 or PEK-1 at high DTT is well-documented. This represents a sophisticated genetic dissection of concentration-dependent toxicity mechanisms.

results.result: DTT is a reducing agent that disrupts ER oxidative protein folding and has been widely used as an ER-specific stressor, though some studies suggest alternative mechanisms including ROS generation and ER-independent effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C118-C126 summarize established knowledge about DTT's properties and effects, all appropriately supported by citations to prior literature. This provides necessary background context for the study. The claims accurately represent the state of knowledge including conflicting views about DTT's mechanism of action.

results.result: DTT toxicity in C. elegans occurs primarily through modulation of the methionine-homocysteine cycle via upregulation of rips-1, leading to SAM depletion. This mechanism extends beyond the ER to affect mitochondrial UPR, challenging the view of DTT as an ER-specific stressor.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C139 represent summary conclusions integrating multiple lines of evidence from the study. The conclusions are well-supported by the experimental data presented. The challenge to DTT being ER-specific (C133-C135) is justified by the mitochondrial UPR data and the genetic screen results showing specific methionine-homocysteine cycle involvement. The concentration-dependent mechanism (C137-C139) is supported by the UPR mutant analysis.

results.result: DTT may be a substrate for RIPS-1 methyltransferase, and upregulation of methyltransferases might represent a general defense response against thiol reagents, analogous to the gliotoxin defense mechanism in fungi.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C141 are explicitly speculative about DTT being a RIPS-1 substrate. While C142 cites evidence that thiols can be methylated, and C144-C147 describe the gliotoxin defense mechanism in fungi, these do not directly demonstrate that DTT is methylated by RIPS-1 in C. elegans. The hypothesis (C148) is reasonable but requires direct biochemical validation of RIPS-1 substrate specificity and DTT methylation.

results.result: The methionine-homocysteine cycle is an important intervention point for health and lifespan, and DTT at non-toxic concentrations might have beneficial effects through modulating this cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C152 appropriately cite literature on the importance of methionine metabolism for health and lifespan. However, C153 is explicitly speculative ("it will be intriguing to test") about potential beneficial effects of low-dose DTT. No data are presented testing this hypothesis. While the speculation is reasonable given that SAM reduction can extend lifespan, this remains untested future work.

results.result: Modulation of the methionine-homocysteine cycle by DTT may be conserved across organisms including A. niger and mammalian cells, based on observations of methyltransferase upregulation and altered cysteine levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C154 and C158 are explicitly speculative ("it is likely possible," "it is possible"). While C155 cites evidence of increased cysteine in DTT-treated mammalian cells and C58 notes methyltransferase upregulation in A. niger, these observations are indirect. The connection between DTT, methyltransferase upregulation, and methionine-homocysteine cycle modulation has only been directly demonstrated in C. elegans in this study. Cross-species conservation requires direct experimental validation.

results.result: Summary of main findings: Dietary vitamin B12 alleviates DTT toxicity through methionine synthase; loss-of-function of rips-1 confers DTT resistance; DTT upregulates rips-1 and modulates the methionine-homocysteine cycle; DTT toxicity results from SAM depletion; IRE-1/XBP-1 UPR is required at high but not low DTT concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C9 are abstract-level summaries of the main findings, each supported by multiple detailed experimental results evaluated above. These represent accurate high-level summaries of well-supported conclusions from the study.
